headline: Super death benefits paid to non-tax-dependants (e.g. adult children) taxed at ~20% plus Medicare levy on the taxable component, creating significant estate-planning trade-offs
reasoning: Death benefits paid to a tax-dependent (spouse or dependent child) are received tax-free, but benefits paid to non-dependants such as adult children attract tax of approximately 20% plus Medicare levy on the taxable component. The taxable component covers past employer (concessional) contributions, which represent the majority of most members' balances; after-tax (non-concessional) contributions pass tax-free regardless of recipient. This creates a meaningful incentive to route benefits via a surviving spouse rather than directly to adult children, though careful pre-planning is required to structure the outcome optimally.
quote: it depends on who they're they're paid to. So if they're paid to someone that's considered a tax dependent, which is generally only like a spouse or a dependent child, then they don't pay tax on the superannuation death benefit received. But if it's paid to non dependent like adult children or any other parties, then normally they pay tax on the the death benefit and that's usually can be around like 20% on the amount that that is paid out. Now it does depend on what your superannuation balance is made up of. So anything that you've ever put in yourself like voluntary, so like after tax contributions, when that gets passed on to someone, no tax is payable. But any part of your superannuation balance that represents like past employer contributions, which for most people is actually the majority of the Super balance that does get taxed at the, at the rate of 20% plus plus Medicare levy. So it's, it's definitely important to think about that in advance because like sometimes what we see, people might want to leave money to their kids, but if they pay to their kids directly, the kids pay tax. So they might instead choose to pay to their spouse and then have the spouse like pass it on to their children.
episode_title: How to avoid a costly super inheritance mistake | the advisory

headline: SMSF trustee incapacity creates legal deadlock if succession arrangements are not in place in advance
reasoning: If an SMSF member loses mental capacity without having appointed an enduring power of attorney (EPA), legal personal representative, or replacement/second trustee beforehand, the fund can be left without anyone legally empowered to manage it. Superannuation rules automatically disqualify a member who loses capacity from acting as trustee, compounding the problem. An EPA alone is insufficient because it covers personal affairs, not the trustee role; the EPA holder must be formally appointed as trustee via paperwork and ATO registration, which can take considerable time. Planning ahead is therefore critical to avoid the fund being stranded without a functioning trustee.
quote: if someone hasn't already appointed like an enduring power of attorney or a legal personal representative or organised like a potential like replacement trustee or a second trustee, that it can actually be quite difficult at that point in time to put those things in place because the person that's supposed to do all those things doesn't have the capacity to do that. So it's just legally it can get quite tricky. And another thing is like, if you no longer have the capacity, the superannuation rules actually say that you're not allowed to act as a trustee anymore. So often like your trustee will actually say that you're, you automatically cease being a trustee when when you seize capacity. So that can make it tricky as well, because then you could end up with a fund that doesn't have someone that's, you know, in the job of actually managing it, like in the job as as trustee.
episode_title: How to avoid a costly super inheritance mistake | the advisory

headline: ATO increasing scrutiny of SMSFs with penalties including personal taxation of unauthorised benefit payments
reasoning: Marjon Muizer of Red Willow Super notes the ATO is cracking down on SMSFs with increased scrutiny around fund expenses and asset valuations. In one example, a trustee spent $25,000 on a forex trading course from a $100,000 fund — roughly a quarter of fund assets — and the ATO treated this as an early release benefit (member lump sum) taxed at 20% plus Medicare levy, regardless of subsequent repayment. The ATO's view is that structuring such payments as loans does not change the taxable nature of the initial outflow. Key compliance messages include maintaining good records throughout the year, ensuring assets are supported by current market valuations at the start of the financial year, and engaging accountants/advisors/auditors early to ensure timely lodgement of returns.
quote: So then what they did is even though that this trustee, they ended up paying the $25,000 back a couple of years later, the ATO, they actually saw the initial payment as like a an early release benefit. So like a member lump sum and they just tax it that way. So they just text it as if you're taking money out of super. Um, and usually the tax rate on the age of 60 is is 20% plus Medicare levy. So they don't really care that you might be putting it back or that you might sort of, you know, structure it as a loan because they just think, well, you you're not supposed to have a loan. So we don't really care how you report it or whether or not you pay it back. They just, um, text you personally as a like as if you've taken the money from from super.
episode_title: SMSFs under increased ATO scrutiny | the advisory
